newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS - Japan urged to twin reforms with safeguards.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Japan urged to twin reforms with safeguards.

text.p: A key Japanese panel called on Friday for a host of securities industry reforms but also stressed the need for tougher penalties for wrongdoers and a stronger watchdog to keep an eye on the liberalised market.

The panel, which is advising the finance minister on "Big Bang" market reforms, recommended giving brokerages more freedom to set their own commission fees and suggested the scrapping of stock taxes which have stifled business.
The interim report by the Securities and Exchange Council is one of several initiatives aimed at mapping out the road to the government's goal of liberalised markets by 2001.

But the report also said reforms should be accompanied by safeguards, such as investment protection for customers, tough penalties for illegal stock deals and a bigger team of regulators to keep financial institutions in line.

Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), was drawn into the spotlight recently by a payoff scandal at Nomura Securities Co Ltd that has once again sullied the reputation of Japanese finance.

In its report, the advisory panel called on the authorities to move swiftly to liberalise commissions on stock transactions in order to trim trading costs to internationally competitive levels. It also said they should consider scrapping taxes on securities deals.
"In order to improve efficiency, Japan needs to fully liberalise commissions on stock transactions of less than 1 billion yen ($8.6 million) as soon as possible, without waiting for 2001," it said.
The move will inject strong competition into the brokerage business and may push some weaker brokerages, already battered by a slumping stock market, to the wall.
Japan should also boost staff numbers at the SESC to improve the body's monitoring ability, it said.

The SESC was set up in 1992 after a scandal in which many brokers improperly recompensed favoured clients for investment losses. Earlier this week the watchdog asked prosecutors to consider criminal charges against Nomura in the latest scandal, which revolves around payments to rackeeters.

The panel recommended harsher penalties for illegal securities deals, in particular insider trading and stock-price manipulation. Critics have said that current penalties including moderate fines and business suspensions are not tough enough to deter wrongdoing.
The panel did not go into detail on what form such tougher penalties might take.

Growing competition as a result of financial liberalisation may expose some brokers to the risk of collapse and it is important to have a mechanism enshrined in the law to compensate investors, the report said.
While the securities industry already runs a voluntary fund to compensate customers in the event of a brokerage collapse, the safety net should be formalised in the law, it said.

The council is scheduled to finalise its proposals for securities reforms in the "Big Bang" package, which aims to invigorate Japan's markets and put them in the same league as thriving financial centres in Europe and America.

In its interim proposals, the panel also called on Japan to allow transactions of listed stocks to be conducted outside the nation's eight stock exchanges, as a spur to competition, and to consider scrapping a licence system for securities brokers in order to open the market up to new players.
The panel also proposed abolishing rules which bar brokers from businesses like asset management, investment trusts, insurance and commodity futures. ($1=116 yen)
